The Northern snakehead (Channa argus) attains a maximum total length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm], based on surveys of large-bodied individuals from its invasive populations in the Potomac River drainage. Field records indicate that the total length at puberty is reached at roughly 30 cm [Lp = roughly 30 cm], marking the onset of gonadal development in this apex predator. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth from fertilised egg to yolk-sac larva emergence is approximately 1.5 days [ab = approximately 1.5 days], a remarkably rapid period of embryonic development typical of tropical channids. The wet weight at birth of freshly eclosed larvae has been measured at 0.0043 grams [Wwb = 0.0043 grams], reflecting the small but nutrient-rich yolk reserves present within the demersal egg.

Reproductive output in Channa argus is substantial, as the species exhibits an iteroparous life-history strategy with high fecundity. During a single spawning event, a gravid female can produce approximately 130,000 to 150,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 130,000 to 150,000 eggs per spawning event]. When the water temperature is stable at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], field observations indicate that the species undertakes up to three discrete spawning events annually [F_R_i = up to three discrete spawning events annually]. Such prolific reproductive capacity, combining large clutch sizes with multiple reproductive bouts per year, underpins the snakehead's success as an invasive species in temperate North American waterways. The energetic investment in each clutch is considerable, as the females must channel substantial resources into the production of thousands of small, lipid-rich oocytes during the breeding season.

The maximum recorded lifespan of the Northern snakehead in captivity, when maintained at 27 °C [T = 27 °C], has been documented at 15 years [am = 15 years]. This extended longevity is characteristic of large-bodied, predatory freshwater teleosts and allows for repeated breeding opportunities across many seasons. The ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown adults has been recorded at 8,000 grams [Wwi = 8,000 grams] in well-nourished individuals from trophy-fishery samples, a value that places this species among the largest freshwater predators in its introduced range. This large body mass requires a substantial foraging territory and a diet rich in fish, crustaceans, and amphibians to sustain its high metabolic demands. The species' life-history strategy thus integrates a long adult phase, slow senescence, and repeated high-fecundity spawning events that collectively drive its population dynamics in both native and introduced ranges.

Sexual maturation in Channa argus is more closely tied to body size than to chronological age, with puberty indicated by a wet weight at puberty of approximately 216 grams [Wwp = approximately 216 grams]. This body mass generally corresponds to individuals that have surpassed the 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] total length threshold, at which point vitellogenesis onset can be detected in females and spermiation onset occurs in males. The allometric relationship between length and mass at this stage is predictable, as the cube-law scaling of body volume dictates a mass of roughly 216 grams for a 30 cm fish. Achieving this size typically requires one to three years depending on prey availability and thermal regime, after which the fish can participate in the annual spawning aggregations. The attainment of this critical body mass thus represents a key life-history checkpoint that determines the species' reproductive contribution to subsequent generations.

Comparative studies among invasive populations reveal that the ultimate total length of 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] in Channa argus is comparable to that observed in the congeneric species Channa micropeltes from Southeast Asia, though the latter can exceed 130 cm. The maximum recorded adult body weight of 8,000 grams [Wwi = 8,000 grams] in Northern snakehead is similarly within the range of large channids but does not reach the extreme sizes documented in the giant snakehead. The species exhibits considerable plasticity in growth rates across its invaded range, with individuals in warm, productive habitats achieving the 100 cm [Li = 100 cm] asymptotic length more rapidly than those in cooler, oligotrophic systems. This environmental sensitivity extends to its metabolic physiology, as the species' maximum reproductive activity is tightly coupled to water temperatures near 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. Overall, the life-history traits of C. argus position it as a highly adaptable, long-lived, and fecund predator capable of establishing dense populations in novel freshwater environments.
